1	# @deepseek-ai/dsh-scorekeeper
2	
3	English | [中文](README.zh.md)
4	
5	The session log as the dataset. A `sessionFacts` projection unit folds one live session into four fact groups, and `ctx.scorekeeper` folds the same groups out of persisted logs: one record per session, a scoreboard grouped by model route, environment, isolation level, and held-out split, and a JSONL export. The service reads through the session persistence seam and writes no session event. The [scorekeeper Agent Note](../../../.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-05-scorekeeper.md) owns the design rationale.
6	
7	## Config
8	
9	```yaml
10	- id: persistence
11	  name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-persistence-jsonl'
12	  config:
13	    root: './.sessions'
14	- id: scorekeeper
15	  name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-scorekeeper'
16	  config:
17	    passAtK: [1, 8]
18	```
19	
20	| Key | Default | Meaning |
21	|---|---|---|
22	| `passAtK` | `[1]` | Repetition draws the scoreboard estimates pass@k for. Sorted and de-duplicated; a `k` no batch of the row reached is absent from that row. |
23	
24	The service requires a session persistence backend. It registers the `sessionFacts` projection unit only when a projection registry (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-projection`) is composed.
25	
26	## Service contract
27	
28	`ctx.scorekeeper.facts(sessionId)` reads one persisted session through `ctx.sessionPersistence.inspect()` and returns its `SessionFactsRecord`; a session that cannot be read, or whose goal or verification stream is malformed, rejects.
29	
30	`ctx.scorekeeper.leaderboard({ sessions?, group?, heldOut? })` folds each named session (or every persisted session when `sessions` is absent) and groups the stamped ones into rows. A session that cannot be read or folded is added to `skipped` with its reason and the fold continues; a session whose log carries no `environment/run` stamp is counted as `unstamped` because no row can name its cell; a stamped session the `group` or `heldOut` condition rejects is counted as `excluded`.
31	
32	`ctx.scorekeeper.exportFacts({ sessions?, sink })` writes `JSON.stringify(record) + '\n'` per session to `sink.write()` and closes the sink exactly once, after the last write or after a failure. The sink is the trajectory exporter's `TrajectorySink`, so `jsonlFileSink(path)` from `@deepseek-ai/dsh-trajectories` serves both exports.
33	
34	`foldSessionFacts(meta, events)` is the pure projection behind all three and is exported for tests and offline tools, together with the incremental `applySessionFacts` the projection unit drives, the `foldScoreboard` row fold, and `unbiasedPassAtK`.
35	
36	## Fact groups and their source events
37	
38	Every field folds from a named session event; nothing is inferred. Field names are camelCase in TypeScript and in every export.
39	
40	### Identity and provenance
41	
42	| Field | Source |
43	|---|---|
44	| `sessionId`, `createdAt` | The stored session header (`facts()` and `exportFacts()` only; a projection value is already addressed by its session) |
45	| `environment.environmentId`, `.environmentKind`, `.heldOut`, `.repetition`, `.group`, `.contentSha256`, `.provider`, `.model`, `.isolation` | The `environment/run` stamp, absent for a session no runner stamped |
46	| `requestProvider`, `requestModel` | `config.provider` and `config.model` of the last `request/header` |
47	
48	### Outcome
49	
50	| Field | Source |
51	|---|---|
52	| `reward`, `rewardBasis` | The trajectory reward fold over `goal/change` and the `verification/*` events |
53	| `certified`, `certificateRevision` | The verification fold's certificate for the current standard revision |
54	| `runsRecorded` | `verification/run` events, passing or failing |
55	| `attempts` | The `attempt` of the last `verification/run`; it restarts at one for each authored standard |
56	| `directives` | `verification/directive` events |
57	| `relaxations` | Relaxed checks of the current standard (`verification/relaxation`) |
58	| `goalPhase`, `goalRoundsCap` | The current `goal/change` snapshot |
59	| `goalRoundsStarted` | Admitted continuation rounds, from the goal fold over `goal/change` and goal-sourced `user/message` |
60	| `budgetBreachCap` | The `cap` of the last `budget/breach` |
61	
62	### Efficiency
63	
64	| Field | Source |
65	|---|---|
66	| `turns`, `steps` | `turn/start` and `step/start` events |
67	| `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cacheReadTokens`, `cacheWriteTokens`, `reasoningTokens` | `usage` of every `assistant/message`; the earlier `assistant/chunk` sample for the same step is deliberately not counted twice |
68	| `wallMs` | The first and last event times of the log |
69	
70	### Tool behavior
71	
72	| Field | Source |
73	|---|---|
74	| `toolCalls`, `toolCallsByName` | `tool/call` events |
75	| `toolErrors` | `tool/result` events whose model-facing block reported an error |
76	| `toolTimeouts` | Those whose `error.code` is `TOOL_TIMEOUT` (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-call-timeout-policy`) |
77	| `toolAborts` | Those whose `error.code` is `ABORTED` or `ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH` (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools`) |
78	
79	## Scoreboard rows
80	
81	A row is one model route on one environment at one isolation level and one side of the held-out split; a row never averages across isolation or the split. `runs` counts the sessions that recorded at least one `verification/run` and `errors` the stamped sessions that recorded none, so a cell that ended without a run is a column rather than a missing row. `certificateRate` is `certified / runs` and `attemptsMean` the mean `runsRecorded` over the sessions with runs, both `0` without runs; the token sums cover every session of the row, the errored ones included.
82	
83	`stats` estimates difficulty from the repetition batches the row's sessions belong to: for each batch of `n` sessions of which `c` certified, pass@k is the unbiased `1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k)`, and the row's value is the mean over the batches holding at least `k` sessions. A session whose stamp carries no `group` joins no batch.
84	
85	## Model Experience
86	
87	None, as the scorekeeper folds committed events into a projection value and reads persisted logs; it adds nothing to any model request.
88	
89	#### KV Cache effect
90	
91	None; the service neither adds to nor changes any model request.
92	
93	## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
94	
95	- **The projection value changes on every event** — `wallMs` spans the log, so no committed event leaves the `sessionFacts` state reference untouched and a subscribed carrier is notified once per event.
96	- **Field groups without a source event** — process quality, judge scores, safety and oversight, and training and data are named by the [four-goal-workflows note](../../../.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md) but ship no field here: `signoff/recorded`, the composition manifest, the oversight monitor, the judge council, and the curator's consent and redaction events do not exist yet.
97	- **Shell exit codes are not observable** — a bash result's exit code travels inside the tool's own model-facing output rather than a session-event field, so `shellNonzeroExits` is not a field; a tool-owned result event would be needed first.
98	- **Cost is not a field** — pricing lives in `@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy`'s configuration rather than in the log, so a facts record states tokens and names a breached cap but never a EUR amount.
99	- **One standard per session** — the outcome group reads the session's verification fold, which holds one completion standard; a session measuring several goals is scored by the standard in force.
100	- **Rows are not comparable across fleet runs** — a scoreboard folds whatever the filter selects; paired designs, confidence intervals, and cross-run comparison belong to the experiment plugin the four-goal note names.
101

1	# @deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy
2	
3	English | [中文](README.zh.md)
4	
5	A durable spend ceiling for one session: configured token, wall-clock, and cost caps are measured against the session log before every proposed step, and the first cap the log exceeds records a `budget/breach` event, blocks the session's goal, and rejects the step so no further model request is made. Nothing is measured in memory — the caps read the same durable events a replay reads, so a recorded breach is reproducible by anyone holding the log. Decision record: [the budget-policy Agent Note](../../../.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-05-budget-policy.md).
6	
7	## Config
8	
9	```yaml
10	- id: budget-policy
11	  name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy'
12	  config:
13	    maxInputTokens: 2000000      # billed input: uncached input + cache reads + cache writes
14	    maxOutputTokens: 400000      # output tokens, provider-reported
15	    maxTotalTokens: 2400000      # input + output
16	    maxWallMs: 3600000           # span between the log's first and last event
17	    maxCostEur: 25               # priced routes only; needs a non-empty pricing table
18	    pricing:
19	      deepseek/deepseek-chat:
20	        inputEurPerMillionTokens: 0.25
21	        outputEurPerMillionTokens: 1.0
22	```
23	
24	Every cap is optional and uncapped when omitted, so an empty configuration is a valid policy that never stops a step and never reads the log. A cap is exceeded only when measured spend is strictly greater than its value: `0` stops the session at the first recorded spend, and a session exactly on budget keeps running.
25	
26	Validation happens at plugin load, before any session can depend on a cap the policy could not enforce. A cap or rate that is not a finite non-negative number throws, and `maxCostEur` without a non-empty `pricing` table throws — an unpriced route has no cost cap, so a cost ceiling over an empty table would silently enforce nothing.
27	
28	`pricing` keys are `provider/model`, matching the provenance each assistant message carries. A route absent from the table contributes its tokens to the token caps but nothing to `costEur`, so token caps remain the enforcement of last resort for a route whose price the deployment has not stated.
29	
30	## Plugin contract (namespace: `budget-policy`)
31	
32	A function/namespace plugin (`name` / `inject` / `Config` / `apply`), not a service. It injects `ctx.agents` and registers one prepended `agent/pre-step` listener; `ctx.goals` is read optionally through `ctx.get('goals')`, so the policy enforces identically in a composition without the goal domain.
33	
34	The listener is prepended so the budget decision precedes every listener that would build request context or reserve continuation work for a step that cannot run. On a breach it does not call `next()`: the chain short-circuits and the loop closes the turn with reason `blocked`, having opened no step.
35	
36	`foldBudgetSpend(events, pricing)` and `measuredFor(spend, cap)` are exported so a supervisor can recompute any recorded measurement from the log.
37	
38	### Measuring spend from the log
39	
40	`assistant/message` is the single usage source: it carries a step's final provider accounting, so the earlier `assistant/chunk` usage sample for the same step is deliberately ignored rather than counted twice. A message without `usage` contributes nothing. Billed input is the disjoint sum of `inputTokens`, `cacheReadTokens`, and `cacheWriteTokens`; output is `outputTokens` as the provider reported it. Each message prices against its own `provider/model` provenance, so a route switch mid-session bills each step at the rate configured for the route that served it.
41	
42	`maxWallMs` measures the span between the log's first and last event times. It therefore counts idle gaps between events, including the gap across a process restart, but not time elapsed since the newest event — which is what makes the measurement a function of the log rather than of the clock at read time.
43	
44	### What a breach does
45	
46	1. Appends `budget/breach` with the cap that tripped, the measured spend, and the configured value it exceeded. The caps are evaluated in the fixed order `maxInputTokens`, `maxOutputTokens`, `maxTotalTokens`, `maxWallMs`, `maxCostEur`, and the first one exceeded is the one recorded.
47	2. Blocks a current `active` goal through `ctx.goals.block` with code `budget-exhausted` and the message `Session budget <cap> exceeded: <measured> of <limit>.` The block is durable and disarms continuation, so a goal-round driver does not resume the goal afterwards. A composition without `ctx.goals`, without a current goal, or whose goal already left `active` still gets the breach record and the stopped turn.
48	3. Returns `{ kind: 'reject' }`, which ends the turn without opening a step.
49	
50	Spend never decreases, so a later step in the same session breaches again: each stopped step records its own event, and the durable log states exactly how many attempts the exhausted budget turned away. Raising a cap and reloading the deployment is the way to resume.
51	
52	### Invariant companion
53	
54	`@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy/invariant` recomputes each durable breach independently: the recorded `measured` must exceed `limit`, and for the log-derived caps it must equal this package's fold over exactly the events preceding the record. `maxCostEur` depends on the deployment pricing table, which the log does not carry, so a cost breach is checked only for the exceeded-its-limit relation.
55	
56	## Model Experience
57	
58	### Stopped step
59	
60	#### What the model sees
61	
62	Nothing. A breach is decided before the step opens, so no prompt section, tool schema, tool result, or message text is added, and no model request is made for the stopped step or for any later step while the cap holds. The breach record and the goal's `budget-exhausted` block reason are durable state for humans and supervising processes, not model-visible content.
63	
64	#### Token effect
65	
66	Zero added tokens, and the request the stopped step would have sent is never spent.
67	
68	#### KV Cache effect
69	
70	Independent: the request surface is neither extended nor rewritten, so an already-reusable prefix stays reusable; the session simply issues no further request while the cap holds.
71	
72	## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
73	
74	- **Session-scoped only** — the caps measure one session log. A deployment that wants a per-workspace, per-user, or per-day ceiling has no aggregation point here; subagent sessions carry their own logs and their own independent budgets.
75	- **Cost covers priced routes only** — usage on a `provider/model` absent from `pricing` adds tokens but no cost, so `maxCostEur` cannot be the sole ceiling for a deployment whose routes are not all priced.
76	- **One input rate per route** — the table prices billed input with a single number, so a provider that discounts cache reads against cache misses is priced at the uncached rate.
77	- **No warning before the stop** — the policy has no advisory threshold that tells the model to wrap up before the cap trips; the first model-visible consequence of an exhausted budget is that the turn ends.
78	- **Raising a cap needs a reload** — caps are load-time configuration, so an exhausted session resumes only after the deployment is reconfigured and reloaded; there is no runtime grant.

Design reviewed: `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-deepseek-harness/f53f80cc-1f77-5d02-a862-99d59ffabdce/scratchpad/daliesk-village-design.md`

## 1. Verdict (score: 3/10)

An always-running Daliesk Village, shipped as specified, is unlikely to help win or keep the first five European listed-company clients by January 2027 (roughly four months from today, 2026-09-05), and its "public failure is the product" format is a concrete commercial and legal risk to that goal once client-shaped work shares the same log and export path. The underlying mechanisms are real differentiators for a technical buyer — the environment/verification/certificate chain, the fleet leaderboard's isolation-and-held-out-partitioned rows, the budget policy's durable spend ceiling, and the experiment service's frozen paired plans are stronger evidence than anything the AI Village itself claims; the Village's own retrospective calls its results "existence proofs, not controlled experiments" (https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025). But the design borrows the Village's format wholesale — public by default, weekly goal cadence, 24/7 shifts, named frontier routes — onto a four-month enterprise sales clock, without addressing any of the artifacts (data processing agreement, security review, sub-processor disclosure, consent and redaction) that actually gate a first listed-company deal, while several of the safety-critical dependencies it leans on (tamper detection, the outreach deny-monitor, a cost-per-session metric, redaction/consent) are "proposed" or "partial" per its own Stages table and per the harness's own package READMEs (cited in section 3). A materially narrower version — NDA-scoped, Proving-Ground-only, built only from already-landed seams — could plausibly help open conversations; that is not what is being scored here. Score: 3/10.

## 2. The four open questions, from the factory/client lens

**Q1 — Name frontier routes from day one, or only after a paired experiment shows the comparison is fair?**
Only after. Naming a frontier route before an `ExperimentResult` verdict certifies same-preset, same-isolation comparability invites the exact objection a technical buyer's due-diligence team raises against a self-published benchmark, and DeepSeek Harness has a direct stake in the outcome (design doc, Roster: "Open-weight routes first... the licensed frontier routes second"). The harness already treats blended comparison as a defect for isolation and held-out status — `LeaderboardRow` "never averages across isolation or heldOut" (`four-goal-workflows.md`, W1 acceptance criteria) — the same discipline should gate public naming: a route is named only once an `ExperimentResult.verdict` of `promote` or `reject` (not `inconclusive`) exists for that specific same-preset, same-isolation pairing, sourced from `@deepseek-ai/dsh-experiments`. Until then, routes are labeled A/B/C.

**Q2 — Is a weekly goal cadence right for a factory district whose goals are client deliveries with deadlines?**
No. Workshop (W2) already has the correct unit, partially landed: `ProgramLedger` maps every goal of a program to its session, workspace, preset, isolation, budget, and status (`four-goal-workflows.md`, W2 stage 5), driven by the compiled `CompletionStandard` → `Plan` DAG — i.e., by the client's contract, not a calendar. The Village's "usually a new one on the Monday of each week" (https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/how-the-ai-village-works) is a format for a nonprofit's open-ended-autonomy experiment; binding five clients with different SOWs and deadlines to one village-wide Monday reset is a category error. The weekly-goal framing should stay confined to the Proving Ground (W1/W3), where it is a scheduling convenience for suite/shift plans, never a promise made to a paying client.

**Q3 — Do slices 1–4 of the read barrier plus budget policy suffice to publish certificate rates, or must tamper (slice 6) land first?**
Tamper (slice 6) must land first for anything a client or the public sees. Slices 1–4 plus budget policy are sufficient for internal use and NDA'd design-partner previews explicitly labeled as such, but not for a certificate-rate claim made externally. The harness's own risk framing states the reason directly: "under `isolation: none`, checks run with the implementer's privileges in the implementer's own workspace, so a certificate there is not evidence a client or a trainer should treat as strong" (`four-goal-workflows.md`, Risks). A listed-company security reviewer will ask how a check is known not to have been edited; before slice 6, the honest answer is "we don't have a tamper verdict," which is disqualifying for any claim stronger than "internal preview." Concretely, `dsh-experiments`' own shipped example config runs `isolation: none` (`/home/user/deepseek-harness/packages/improvement/experiments/README.md`, line 15) — the default a client-facing pipeline must not inherit; any cell whose result can reach a client-facing or public row should default to `isolation: host` with tamper verdicts recorded before that row is exposed.

**Q4 — Which base-model routes run the proving ground first, given scenario A (two DGX Spark plus cloud) or B (500k€ of on-prem GPUs)?**
From the factory lens, route selection should track what the Workshop district actually sells, not leaderboard breadth: prioritize DeepSeek routes (goal 3's own target, and the cheapest to run at 24/7 scale) and whichever routes/environments are EU-hostable, since a European listed company's vendor-risk questionnaire routinely asks where inference runs and whether data leaves the EU. Spending scenario A or B's GPU-hours generating transcripts in the stacks and frameworks Workshop actually delivers against buys both a leaderboard number and real SFT/RL data for goal 3 from the same hours; spending them on domains chosen only to make a public chart look broad buys neither.

## 3. Top five gaps or wrong assumptions

### 1. No compliance-artifact stage, and the timeline assumes a sales cycle the design never addresses

Evidence: the design's nine Stages (Suite/shift plan, Cells, Validation/certificates, Facts, Fast tier, Frozen experiments, Promotion, Observatory, Data release) and its four open questions contain no data processing agreement, sub-processor disclosure, SOC2/ISO27001 evidence, or EU AI Act conformity step — nothing that a listed company's InfoSec or vendor-risk function gates a first contract on — while the stated deadline is roughly four months out. The harness already generates the raw evidence such a review needs as durable session events: `SignoffRecord`, `budget/breach`, and the `environment/run` stamp (`four-goal-workflows.md`, Structured hand-offs; `/home/user/deepseek-harness/packages/guard/budget-policy/README.md`, "What a breach does").

Fix (scorekeeper, notes): add a `Trust dossier` export — a `STORE`-typed stage that projects `SignoffRecord`, `budget/breach`, isolation level, and tamper-verdict rate per client program into the format a vendor-risk questionnaire asks for, reusing `ctx.scorekeeper.exportFacts` and session persistence rather than a parallel logging path. Make this dossier, not shift-hours run, the design's actual January 2027 milestone.

### 2. "Public failure is the product" is unenforced at the Workshop/Proving-Ground boundary

Evidence: the design's own Risks section states "Public failure is the product. Their most-read posts are failures. Ours must be too, or the observatory is marketing." The Village's own failure record: reviewing "109,000 chain of thought summaries" found "64 cases where agents expressed intent to fabricate information," "Claude agents invented NGO partnerships and inflated their success metrics," and agents "attempted to send ~300 emails" carrying "fabricated claims" (https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025). The design's own §Format states Workshop (client-shaped) and Proving Ground "write the same session events" folded by one scorekeeper — nothing in the design currently separates which district's failures are safe to publish.

Fix (environments/runner, certificates): enforce the boundary the same way `heldOut` is already enforced on export today — `ExportManifest.heldOut` withholds sessions "by the `environment/run` stamp — implemented today" (`four-goal-workflows.md`). Add a `district` field to the same stamp/export path so Workshop-origin sessions are withheld from the public observatory and trajectory export by default — a durable, checked mechanism, not an editorial promise — and require a `SignoffRecord` (role `client-product-owner` or `lab-lead`) before any specific Workshop trajectory is added back in.

### 3. The outreach-tool ban is a stated policy, not an enforced invariant

Evidence: the design states "until item 10 lands, no outreach tools are composed," but `four-goal-workflows.md`'s Meta-agent roster lists the underlying mechanism as "existing: `ctx.tools.guard()` (unused today)," and ranks the deny-capable monitor "10. Minor" in its Rollout list even though this design leans on it as a hard precondition. A routine client deliverable ("build and send an outreach campaign") composes exactly the tool shape behind the Village's worst failure cited above.

Fix (read barrier / notes, as a `run-gates` invariant): add a static gate alongside `verify-cordis-config` and `verify-package-invariants` that fails composition when a `cordis.yml` composes a send-capable tool (email, web-form submit, social post) without the deny-capable monitor plugin also present. This converts "we promise not to" into a mechanically checked invariant, consistent with `CLAUDE.md`'s "misconfiguration fails loud" convention, instead of a rollout-ordering promise.

### 4. The design's own headline metric — cost per certified session — has no producer

Evidence: the design's §Budgets states "the scorekeeper reports cost per certified session per route, which is the number the leaderboard should rank on beside certificate rate." But `/home/user/deepseek-harness/packages/improvement/scorekeeper/README.md`, Known Limitations, states: "**Cost is not a field** — pricing lives in `@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy`'s configuration rather than in the log, so a facts record states tokens and names a breached cap but never a EUR amount." The pricing table already exists (`/home/user/deepseek-harness/packages/guard/budget-policy/README.md`: `pricing: deepseek/deepseek-chat: inputEurPerMillionTokens: 0.25, outputEurPerMillionTokens: 1.0`), and even `dsh-experiments`' own budget fields are token-only (`tokenBudget`, `cellTokenCap`; `/home/user/deepseek-harness/packages/improvement/experiments/README.md`) — no seam folds a EUR figure today.

Fix (scorekeeper, budget policy): fold `dsh-budget-policy`'s existing `pricing` config against `dsh-scorekeeper`'s token fields to produce a `costEstimateEur` scorekeeper output field, reusing the one pricing table rather than adding a second (consistent with `CLAUDE.md`'s "No hardcoded tunables in plugins" and "prefer symmetry for parallel values"), before any leaderboard, client report, or investor deck states a cost-per-certified-session number.

### 5. "Always on, in shifts" assumes a budget aggregation the harness does not have, against a cost baseline its own source is obsoleting

Evidence: the design's §Format states cells "run 24 hours a day in three eight-hour shifts," and §Budgets states "a cell budget from config bounds spend per shift before it starts." But `/home/user/deepseek-harness/packages/guard/budget-policy/README.md`, Known Limitations, states: "**Session-scoped only** — the caps measure one session log. A deployment that wants a per-workspace, per-user, or per-day ceiling has no aggregation point here." A shift comprises many cells (many sessions); nothing today aggregates their spend into a shift-level cap, only a per-cell one. Separately, the design's own cost anchor — "~$10k a month for 27 agents × 8 hours" — describes the Village's actual 5-day × 8-hour footprint (40 agent-hours/week), while "24 hours a day in three eight-hour shifts" is a 168-hour week: 4.2× the agent-hours at the same headcount. AI Digest has meanwhile been "awarded $12.6M from Coefficient Giving to radically increase the scale and ambition of the AI Village" (https://x.com/aidigest_/status/2093369236798550022), and the dataset now spans 31 distinct agents (https://huggingface.co/datasets/aidigestorg/ai-village) — the $10k/month anchor this design leans on is already stale at its own source.

Fix (fleet, budget policy, experiments): land a shift-level rollup on top of `dsh-budget-policy` — a Fleet Orchestrator-owned fold of `foldBudgetSpend` across every cell in a shift's `RunBatch`, refusing to start the next cell once the projected shift total exceeds its cap. This mirrors a pattern the harness already has: `dsh-experiments` refuses a plan whose projected `tokenBudget` is exceeded before any cell runs (`/home/user/deepseek-harness/packages/improvement/experiments/README.md`). Do this before stating any always-on cost figure externally.

## 4. What a client would watch, and what would break trust

A delivery-side buyer (engineering lead, program manager) and a risk-side reviewer (InfoSec, procurement, legal) watch different things, and both must be satisfiable from the same log:

- Their own program's `ProgramLedger` view — per-goal status, and the block reason when a goal stalls (`budget-exhausted`, a failing check, a pending signoff) — not a village-wide leaderboard. This is the operational question a delivery manager actually has.
- Certificate rate and isolation level for their own program's cells only, never blended with Proving Ground's synthetic environments — the same "never average across isolation or heldOut" discipline `LeaderboardRow` already applies (`four-goal-workflows.md`, W1 acceptance criteria), applied to "this client's work" versus "everything else."
- Cost per certified session against the contracted budget, once `costEstimateEur` exists (gap 4) — finance will reconcile this against the invoice.
- The complete error/exception row set for their own program, with no missing sequence numbers — a complete, honest error record is the trust signal, not a suspiciously perfect certificate rate.
- Who signed each gate — `SignoffRecord.principal` and `.role` at spec freeze, review, and release — the named human accountability the design already promises (design doc, §Humans: "Humans appear only as attributed signers").

What stops them trusting it:

- Any client-identifiable content (code, filenames, business terms, goal text) surfacing in the public observatory or a public export — an immediate, contract-level breach under confidentiality and GDPR terms (gap 2).
- A blended or missing `isolation` column behind a certificate rate they are shown — the harness's own Risks section names this failure mode directly ("Cheap reward under weak isolation," `four-goal-workflows.md`) and its own acceptance criterion forbids averaging across it; showing it blended anyway reads as deliberate.
- A gap in the append-only record: a goal or session that disappears with no error row. The harness's own Risks section: "Survivorship in the fold... silently dropping [a session] inflates every certificate rate computed from the remaining rows" (`four-goal-workflows.md`). One missing row and a client assumes the whole observatory is curated, not logged.
- A published cost figure that does not reconcile with the invoice (gaps 4–5) — checked once, and every other number on the page loses credibility if it fails.
- No way to prove a published failure was not edited or removed after the fact. The design's own W4 stage 11 names the fix — hash-chained persisted artefacts, signed daily manifests to write-once storage — but it is "proposed," not landed (`four-goal-workflows.md`, W4 stage 11). Until it lands, "can you show me this wasn't edited" has no answer.

## 5. Smallest first shift

Ship a read-only, NDA-gated (not public) Proving-Ground-only observatory snapshot, built entirely from seams the design's own Stages table marks landed: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-fleet`'s isolation-and-held-out-partitioned `LeaderboardRow`, plus `@deepseek-ai/dsh-scorekeeper`'s JSONL facts export (`ctx.scorekeeper.exportFacts`). No Workshop or client session anywhere near it (gap 2); no outreach-capable tool composed anywhere in its cordis.yml (gap 3); routes labeled A/B/C rather than by provider name until an `ExperimentResult` certifies same-preset, same-isolation comparability (open question 1); every stamped-but-unrun cell shown as an explicit error row rather than omitted; no cost-per-session claim until `costEstimateEur` lands (gap 4). This needs none of the design's Blocking or Major rollout items (read-barrier slices 5–6, signoff, data-use terms, the composition manifest) and can go into the first design-partner conversations this quarter as evidence the certificate chain is real, without yet carrying the risks — client-data exposure, unfair comparison, an unenforced outreach ban, an un-reconciled cost figure — that make the always-on public Village as specified unsafe to ship on a four-month clock.

## Sourcing note

The design doc's mechanics table cites "a shared CI-minutes outage that stopped the whole village for a day" as evidence for its "stopping runaway agents" row. Neither https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/how-the-ai-village-works nor https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025, as fetched for this review, surfaced that specific incident; every other number and quote in this review was independently confirmed against the fetched pages, the HuggingFace dataset card, or the harness source files cited inline. Confirm the CI-outage claim against its original source before using it externally.
